arXiv:2609.33491v1 [math.AG] 27 Sep 2026

Coordinate descents, monodromy, and finite normalization
of marked-root maps

José A. R. Fonollosa ††thanks: Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain. jose.fonollosa@upc.edu. ORCID: 0000-0001-9513-7939.
September 2026
Abstract

We study the dimension-indexed marked-root polynomial maps introduced by Harish. For every n≥4n\geq 4, their lower coefficient block extends to a polynomial coordinate system, giving three-dimensional Keller maps of geometric degree n⁡(n−2)n(n-2) for every choice of the fixed coefficients. We determine the generic monodromy of the original maps and all successive coordinate descents: it is the cyclic wreath product for odd nn, and an explicit subgroup of index two for even nn. Its order is (n−2)n​n!/gcd⁡(2,n−2)(n-2)^{n}n!/\gcd(2,n-2). We construct the smooth finite normalization and identify its complement of the affine source as n−2n-2 disjoint affine divisors. One is ramified; the others record unramified loss of inverse sheets. The normalization has Picard group ℤn−2\mathbb{Z}^{n-2} and the homotopy type of a wedge of n−2n-2 two-spheres. Its rational deck group is cyclic, while the polynomial deck group of the source map is trivial. By base change, the normalization describes the preimage of any subvariety of the target; when the target polynomial factors, a component with only constant units is an open subset of a Kummer cover of the simple roots of one factor. Finally, the monodromy separates these maps, for n≥4n\geq 4, from single weighted lifts under stable polynomial left–right equivalence.

Keywords: Keller maps, Jacobian conjecture, coordinate descent, monodromy, finite normalization.

MSC 2020: 14R15 (primary); 14R10, 14E20, 12F10 (secondary).

1 Introduction and principal results

All varieties and function fields are over ℂ\mathbb{C}.

1.1 Keller maps and the marked-root construction

A Keller map is a polynomial map F:𝔸n→𝔸nF:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant. Such a map is a local analytic isomorphism at every point, and the Jacobian conjecture, going back to Keller [8], asserts that it is then a global polynomial automorphism; see [2, 13] for background. Two numerical invariants recur throughout:

  • •

    the geometric degree of FF, which is the degree of its function-field extension ℂ⁡(𝔸n)/F∗​ℂ​(𝔸n)\mathbb{C}(\mathbb{A}^{n})/F^{*}\mathbb{C}(\mathbb{A}^{n}), or equivalently the number of points in a generic fibre;

  • •

    its generic monodromy, the permutation group of the sheets over a small open subset of the target.

The geometric degree should not be confused with the degrees of the coordinate polynomials. A Keller map is an automorphism exactly when its geometric degree is one.

Harish constructed, for every n≥3n\geq 3, Keller maps Kn:𝔸n→𝔸nK_{n}:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} of geometric degree n⁡(n−2)n(n-2) [5]. Since n⁡(n−2)>1n(n-2)>1, each KnK_{n} is a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture in dimension nn. The conjecture in dimension two remains open, and this is what makes the lower-dimensional restrictions of KnK_{n} studied here interesting. The idea of the construction is easiest to state on the target side.

  • •

    A target point is a polynomial P⁡(T)P(T) of degree at most nn whose coefficient of TT equals one; its remaining nn coefficients are the target coordinates.

  • •

    A generic source point over PP is a pair (t,a)(t,a) consisting of a root tt of PP and a marking aa with an−2=P′​(t)a^{n-2}=P^{\prime}(t).

For a generic PP there are nn roots and n−2n-2 markings for each, which explains the degree n⁡(n−2)n(n-2). The source coordinates are recovered from (t,a)(t,a) by explicit formulas, recalled in Section 2. The construction, the constant Jacobian, the complete fibre formula, the image and the nonproperness locus of KnK_{n} (the set of target points near which the map fails to be proper [7]) are due to Harish; we recall the construction with full derivations to fix conventions.

For the original cubic example, a coordinate-free recognition of the affine source and a precise tangency criterion appear in [14, Appendix A]. The present paper concerns the whole dimension-indexed family.

1.2 Questions addressed

The description by roots and markings raises three natural questions.

  1. 1.

    Descent. Fixing some target coefficients restricts KnK_{n} to a subfamily. Is each such restriction again a Keller map on an affine space, so that one obtains Keller maps in dimension three?

  2. 2.

    Monodromy. The root-and-marking description suggests the wreath product μn−2≀Sn\mu_{n-2}\wr S_{n} as monodromy group, but the markings may satisfy relations. What is the actual group, and is it preserved by specialization?

  3. 3.

    Completion. Rational inverse formulas describe sheets that escape to infinity only after one knows which finite completion the source sits in. What is the finite normalization, and which divisors are missing from the source?

1.3 Notation

Put m=n−2m=n-2. We name the target coefficients by

P⁡(T)=q​Tn+r​Tn−1+∑j=2n−2λj​Tj+T−b.P(T)=qT^{n}+rT^{n-1}+\sum_{j=2}^{n-2}\lambda_{j}T^{j}+T-b. (1)

For n=3n=3 the sum is empty, and (r,q,b)=(A2,C3,A0)(r,q,b)=(A_{2},C_{3},A_{0}). For n≥4n\geq 4, Section 2 writes the same coefficients as Cn=qC_{n}=q, Cn−1=rC_{n-1}=r, Cj=λjC_{j}=\lambda_{j} for 3≤j≤n−23\leq j\leq n-2, A2=λ2A_{2}=\lambda_{2} and A0=bA_{0}=b.

The coefficients λ2,…,λn−2\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2} are called the lower coefficients. A successive coordinate descent fixes a prefix λ2,…,λk\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k} to complex values and keeps the remaining lower coefficients and r,q,br,q,b free. The empty prefix is the original map, up to a permutation of its outputs. We write dd for the dimension of the resulting target, so 3≤d≤n3\leq d\leq n. The case d=3d=3, with all lower coefficients fixed, gives maps to 𝔸r,q,b3\mathbb{A}^{3}_{r,q,b}.

1.4 Principal results

Theorem 1.1 (Polynomial coordinate descent).

For every n≥4n\geq 4, the lower coefficient functions (A2,C3,…,Cn−2)(A_{2},C_{3},\ldots,C_{n-2}) of KnK_{n} are part of a polynomial coordinate system on its source. The coordinate changes and their inverses are constructed recursively, and they fix the source coordinate xx. Consequently every fixed tuple λ∈ℂn−3\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^{n-3} gives a Keller map

En,λ:𝔸3⟶𝔸r,q,b3E_{n,\lambda}:\mathbb{A}^{3}\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{3}_{r,q,b}

of geometric degree n​mnm, in source coordinates (x,sn−1,sn)(x,s_{n-1},s_{n}) constructed in Section 3. The same holds at every intermediate step of a successive descent, for every value of the fixed coefficients.

In other words, after a polynomial change of source coordinates, KnK_{n} becomes a family (λ,ξ)↦(λ,En,λ​(ξ))(\lambda,\xi)\mapsto(\lambda,E_{n,\lambda}(\xi)) parametrized by the lower coefficients. This is not a product with a single map: En,λE_{n,\lambda} genuinely depends on λ\lambda. The proof in Section 3 rests on a simple completion lemma and on the behaviour of the coefficients along the divisor x=0x=0.

The three-dimensional endpoints need not be new equivalence classes of maps. In particular, E4,0E_{4,0} is polynomially left–right equivalent to the degree-eight power-weighted map of [1]; Section 7.1 gives the coordinate identity. Our claim concerns the uniform coordinate completion of the whole family, not the novelty of each resulting map.

Theorem 1.2 (Generic monodromy).

For KnK_{n} and every successive coordinate descent, the monodromy group acting on the n​mnm sheets is

Gn={μmn⋊Sn,n​ odd,{(ζ1,…,ζn,σ)∈μmn⋊Sn:(∏iζi)m/2=sgn⁡(σ)},n​ even.G_{n}=\begin{cases}\mu_{m}^{n}\rtimes S_{n},&n\text{ odd},\\[2.0pt] \bigl\{(\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{n};\sigma)\in\mu_{m}^{n}\rtimes S_{n}:(\prod_{i}\zeta_{i})^{m/2}=\sgn(\sigma)\bigr\},&n\text{ even}.\end{cases} (2)

In particular |Gn|=mn​n!/gcd⁡(2,m)|G_{n}|=m^{n}n!/\gcd(2,m).

Here σ\sigma permutes the roots and ζi\zeta_{i} rotates the marking of the ii-th root. For odd nn every combination occurs. For even nn the markings satisfy one relation, coming from the classical identity between the product of the values P′​(ti)P^{\prime}(t_{i}) and the discriminant; this cuts the wreath product down to an index-two subgroup. We give that subgroup as a subset of the wreath product and do not claim that it splits over SnS_{n}. Yang reported numerical monodromy of order 192192 for K4K_{4} [18]. Our proof obtains this order algebraically and gives the result for all nn and all fixed parameters, by combining valuations at a colliding pair of roots with a Morse specialization (Section 4).

Theorem 1.3 (Finite normalization and boundary).

Let F:𝔸d→Y=𝔸dF:\mathbb{A}^{d}\to Y=\mathbb{A}^{d} be KnK_{n} or a successive coordinate descent, and let ZZ be the normalization of YY in the function field ℂ⁡(𝔸d)\mathbb{C}(\mathbb{A}^{d}) via FF. Then ZZ is smooth and finite flat of degree n​mnm over YY. The source embeds as an open subset U≃𝔸dU\simeq\mathbb{A}^{d} of ZZ, and Z∖UZ\setminus U is a disjoint union of mm copies of 𝔸d−1\mathbb{A}^{d-1}:

  1. 1.

    one critical divisor, with generic ramification index 2​m2m and residue degree one, which normalizes the binary discriminant;

  2. 2.

    m−1m-1 unramified divisors, each mapping isomorphically onto the hyperplane {b=0}\{b=0\} of polynomials that vanish at T=0T=0.

Moreover

Pic⁡(Z)≃ℤm,Z⁡(ℂ)≃⋁j=1mS2.\Pic(Z)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{m},\qquad Z(\mathbb{C})\simeq\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}S^{2}.

The rational deck group over YY is μm\mu_{m}; the polynomial deck automorphism group of FF is trivial.

Geometrically, a source point disappears in two ways. Over the discriminant two roots collide, and the markings of the colliding pair tend to zero; these sheets form the critical divisor. Over b=0b=0 the root t=0t=0 can carry only the marking a=1a=1; the other m−1m-1 markings correspond to points of ZZ at which the source coordinate yy has a pole. Finite normalization is an established tool for Keller maps, see [3], and its use in comparing related constructions is developed by van Rijn [15, 16]. Here we construct the normalization explicitly. Affine-chart gluing has classical precedents for Danielewski–Fieseler surfaces [4], but we do not identify our completion with a member of that class. Triviality of the polynomial deck group holds for every complex affine-space Keller map; the new information is the rational deck group and its action on the source open.

Corollary 1.4 (Stable distinction).

For n≥4n\geq 4, the original map and every successive coordinate descent are stably polynomially left–right inequivalent to any single ordinary weighted lift of the same geometric degree. Here an ordinary weighted lift is a map to 𝔸A,B,C3\mathbb{A}^{3}_{A,B,C} whose source function field is generated over ℂ⁡(A,B,C)\mathbb{C}(A,B,C) by one element ww with minimal polynomial ℋ⁡(w)−B​C​w+c​A​C2\mathcal{H}(w)-BCw+cAC^{2}, where ℋ∈ℂ⁡[w]\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}[w] has degree n​mnm and c≠0c\neq 0.

The reason is that GnG_{n} is imprimitive on its n​mnm sheets (the mm markings of each root form a block), whereas ordinary weighted lifts have full symmetric, hence primitive, monodromy. The symmetric monodromy of ordinary weighted lifts is a prior result [9], and stable comparison through primitive and imprimitive actions has explicit precedents [17]. The corollary applies those tools to the group computed here. It does not distinguish our maps from all power-weighted lifts or from compositions of weighted lifts.

Finally, Section 6 base-changes the normalization along an arbitrary morphism Γ→Y\Gamma\to Y. This describes exactly the preimage of any subvariety of the target (Proposition 6.1), and, for a factorization of the target polynomial over Γ\Gamma, the components carried by one factor (Proposition 6.4). These facts are the natural input for an analysis of plane sections, which is not carried out here.

1.5 Organization

Section 2 recalls the construction and derives its basic identities. Section 3 proves Theorem 1.1, Section 4 Theorem 1.2, and Section 5 Theorem 1.3. Section 6 treats preimages of subvarieties, Section 7 proves Corollary 1.4 and records the overlap with power-weighted lifts, and Section 8 describes the computational checks that accompany the proofs.

2 The marked-root construction

This section recalls Harish’s construction and fibre theorem [5]. We derive every identity used later, so that the remaining sections can be read without the original source.

2.1 Definition

On 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} use coordinates (x,y,z3,…,zn)(x,y,z_{3},\ldots,z_{n}) and put p=1+x​yp=1+xy. Define a polynomial in an auxiliary variable TT by

Φn​(T)=\displaystyle\Phi_{n}(T)={} (1−y​T)n−1​(p​T−x)\displaystyle(1-yT)^{n-1}(pT-x)

Φn​(T)=∑j=3nCj​Tj+A2​T2+T−A0,Kn=(C3,…,Cn,A2,A0):𝔸n→𝔸n.\Phi_{n}(T)=\sum_{j=3}^{n}C_{j}T^{j}+A_{2}T^{2}+T-A_{0},\qquad K_{n}=(C_{3},\ldots,C_{n},A_{2},A_{0}):\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}.

2.4 Determinant and fibres

Proposition 2.2 (Harish).

The Jacobian determinant of KnK_{n} is m/2m/2. For a target polynomial PP with coefficient of TT equal to one, let s⁡(P)s(P) be the number of simple roots of its degree-nn homogenization Ph​(X1,X0)=X0n​P​(X1/X0)P_{h}(X_{1},X_{0})=X_{0}^{n}P(X_{1}/X_{0}) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. Then

#​Kn−1​(P)=m​s​(P)−(m−1)​𝟏P⁡(0)=0.\#K_{n}^{-1}(P)=m\,s(P)-(m-1)\mathbf{1}_{P(0)=0}. (9)

In particular the geometric degree of KnK_{n} is n​mnm.

The fibre formula has a simple reading. Every simple projective root of PP carries mm source points, one for each marking, except the root t=0t=0, which carries only the marking a=1a=1. Multiple roots carry no source points.

The fibres. The source is the disjoint union of three strata: x​p≠0xp\neq 0, x=0x=0 (where p=1p=1), and p=0p=0 (where x≠0x\neq 0). A point of the source determines the projective root [x:p][x:p] of its image, and the three strata correspond to nonzero finite roots, the root t=0t=0, and the root at infinity.

Nonzero finite roots. Let t≠0t\neq 0 be a simple root of PP. Then P′​(t)≠0P^{\prime}(t)\neq 0, so there are exactly mm nonzero choices of aa in (8). All references to a discriminant below mean the degree-nn binary discriminant, including its specializations when the leading coefficient vanishes.

3 Polynomial coordinates and descent to dimension three

Throughout this section n≥4n\geq 4 and c2=−m/2c_{2}=-m/2. We want new polynomial coordinates on the source of KnK_{n} in which the lower coefficients A2,C3,…,Cn−2A_{2},C_{3},\ldots,C_{n-2} are themselves coordinates. Away from x=0x=0 this is easy: by (4), CkC_{k} contains zk+2z_{k+2} with coefficient x2x^{2}, so one may solve for zk+2z_{k+2} after inverting xx. The whole difficulty is to avoid the denominators x−2x^{-2}, that is, to control the divisor x=0x=0.

Two facts make this possible. By (6), along x=0x=0 every lower coefficient is a source coordinate plus a function of yy. And the coefficient of zk+2z_{k+2} in CkC_{k} is exactly x2x^{2}, with no other occurrence of zk+2z_{k+2}. Lemma 3.1 below shows that these two facts are enough to turn CkC_{k} into a coordinate. The coefficient A2A_{2} has a slightly different shape and is treated first, by a unimodular matrix.

The model case is f=u+x​u2+x2​zf=u+xu^{2}+x^{2}z in ℂ⁡[x,u,z]\mathbb{C}[x,u,z]. Keeping those coefficients as variables, rather than substituting numerical values, gives a polynomial automorphism of the entire source. The offsets are explicit but grow quickly; only their dependence matters. Because these are identities over the polynomial ring in the coefficient coordinates, specializing any prefix to any complex values preserves both inverse identities. No exceptional parameter values are excluded.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Let Θ\Theta be the inverse of the composite coordinate change constructed above, so that it expresses the original source coordinates in the new ones. In these coordinates the lower coefficients are coordinate functions, so, after reordering source and target coordinates,

Kn∘Θ:(λ,ξ)⟼(λ,En,λ​(ξ)),ξ=(x,sn−1,sn).K_{n}\circ\Theta:(\lambda,\xi)\longmapsto(\lambda,E_{n,\lambda}(\xi)),\qquad\xi=(x,s_{n-1},s_{n}).

Its Jacobian matrix is block lower triangular, with an identity block for λ\lambda and the block ∂En,λ/∂ξ\partial E_{n,\lambda}/\partial\xi. Since detJ​Kn=m/2\det JK_{n}=m/2 and detJ​Θ\det J\Theta is a nonzero constant, so is det∂En,λ/∂ξ\det\partial E_{n,\lambda}/\partial\xi, for every λ\lambda.

The sign can be tracked. Each change keeps its new coordinates in the slots of the old ones, so in the source order (x,v2,…,vn−2,sn−1,sn)(x,v_{2},\ldots,v_{n-2},s_{n-1},s_{n}) the automorphism Θ−1\Theta^{-1} has determinant c2​(−1)n−4c_{2}(-1)^{n-4}, and Kn∘ΘK_{n}\circ\Theta, with outputs in the order of KnK_{n}, has determinant (m/2)/(c2​(−1)n)=(−1)n+1(m/2)/(c_{2}(-1)^{n})=(-1)^{n+1}. Moving A2A_{2} to the front of the outputs contributes (−1)n−2(-1)^{n-2}, and moving xx behind the coefficient coordinates contributes (−1)n−3(-1)^{n-3}. Hence, with ξ=(x,sn−1,sn)\xi=(x,s_{n-1},s_{n}) and output order (Cn−1,Cn,A0)(C_{n-1},C_{n},A_{0}),

det∂En,λ∂ξ=(−1)n.\det\frac{\partial E_{n,\lambda}}{\partial\xi}=(-1)^{n}.

Because Θ\Theta is bijective, the fibre of En,λE_{n,\lambda} over (r,q,b)(r,q,b) is in bijection with the fibre of KnK_{n} over the polynomial (1), and (9) applies unchanged. For every fixed λ\lambda there are polynomials in (1) with q≠0q\neq 0, b≠0b\neq 0 and nn distinct roots: fix q≠0q\neq 0 and rr, and choose b≠0b\neq 0 outside the finitely many critical values of q​Tn+r​Tn−1+∑λj​Tj+TqT^{n}+rT^{n-1}+\sum\lambda_{j}T^{j}+T. Such targets form a nonempty Zariski open set, over which the fibre has n​mnm points. Hence the geometric degree is n​mnm for every parameter. Stopping the induction after fixing any prefix of the lower coefficients gives the same conclusion for the intermediate descents. ∎

The recursive formulas specify the maps without expanding their coordinates into large monomial lists. They also explain why a generic rational elimination would not suffice: solving Ck=λkC_{k}=\lambda_{k} for zk+2z_{k+2} introduces the denominator x2x^{2}, and the completion lemma is precisely what removes it.

4 Exact generic monodromy

The generic monodromy of a dominant, generically finite map is the Galois group of the normal closure of the source function field over the target function field, acting on the embeddings of the source field. Equivalently, it is the monodromy of the finite covering over a sufficiently small nonempty Zariski open set of the target.

4.1 Overview

Let kk be the target function field of KnK_{n} or of one of its descents, and let P∈k⁡[T]P\in k[T] be the generic target polynomial. By Section 2, the source function field is k⁡(t,a)k(t,a), where tt is a root of PP and am=P′​(t)a^{m}=P^{\prime}(t): indeed x=t/ax=t/a and y=(1−a)/ty=(1-a)/t by (7), and the zjz_{j} are then rational in x,yx,y and the target coefficients by the triangular system. The n​mnm sheets over a generic point are the pairs (ti,ζ​ai)(t_{i},\zeta a_{i}), where t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n} are the roots, aia_{i} is one chosen mm-th root of di=P′​(ti)d_{i}=P^{\prime}(t_{i}), and ζ∈μm\zeta\in\mu_{m}.

A monodromy element permutes the roots and then rotates each marking by a root of unity. This gives the upper bound μmn⋊Sn\mu_{m}^{n}\rtimes S_{n}, the wreath product μm≀Sn\mu_{m}\wr S_{n}. The question is which rotations actually occur. By Kummer theory, this is governed by multiplicative relations among the did_{i} modulo mm-th powers. We detect such relations with valuations at which exactly two roots collide (Lemma 4.1), and we produce these valuations, together with the full symmetric group on the roots, from a single line in the target space (Lemma 4.2). The only relation that survives comes from the classical identity (14) between the product of the did_{i} and the discriminant. It exists exactly when mm is even, and it cuts the group down by a factor of two.

4.2 Pair valuations and the derivative-root extension

Lemma 4.1.

Let kk be a function field over ℂ\mathbb{C} and P=q​∏i=1n(T−ti)∈k⁡[T]P=q\prod_{i=1}^{n}(T-t_{i})\in k[T], with splitting field k~\tilde{k} and Gal⁡(k~/k)=Sn\Gal(\tilde{k}/k)=S_{n}. Put m=n−2m=n-2. Suppose k~\tilde{k} has a discrete valuation, trivial on ℂ\mathbb{C}, at which qq is a unit, one root difference has value one, and every other root difference has value zero. Let L=k~​(a1,…,an)L=\tilde{k}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}) with aim=P′​(ti)a_{i}^{m}=P^{\prime}(t_{i}). Then L/kL/k is Galois, and Gal⁡(L/k)\Gal(L/k), acting on the n​mnm pairs (ti,ζ​ai)(t_{i},\zeta a_{i}), is the group GnG_{n} of (2). This action is transitive, so the field k⁡(t1,a1)k(t_{1},a_{1}) has degree n​mnm over kk and LL is its normal closure.

Now consider the group of relations

ℛ={(ℓi)∈(ℤ/m)n:∏idiℓi∈k~×m}.\mathcal{R}=\left\{(\ell_{i})\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^{n}:\prod_{i}d_{i}^{\ell_{i}}\in\tilde{k}^{\times m}\right\}.

∏idi=qn​∏i∏j≠i(ti−tj)=(−1)n⁡(n−1)/2​qn​δ2.\prod_{i}d_{i}=q^{n}\prod_{i}\prod_{j\neq i}(t_{i}-t_{j})=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}q^{n}\delta^{2}. (14)

For m=1m=1 the lemma simply describes the root splitting field. ∎

4.3 A Morse line for every fixed coefficient tuple

A polynomial g∈ℂ⁡[T]g\in\mathbb{C}[T] is called Morse if its critical points are simple and its critical values are pairwise distinct. The branched cover g:𝔸T1→𝔸b1g:\mathbb{A}^{1}_{T}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{b} of such a polynomial has local monodromy a transposition around each critical value, and its monodromy group is the full symmetric group [10, Theorem 4.4.5]; the argument is recalled below.

Lemma 4.2.

For any λ2,…,λn−2∈ℂ\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2}\in\mathbb{C}, the polynomial (1) over ℂ⁡(r,q,b)\mathbb{C}(r,q,b) has root group SnS_{n} and a valuation satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 4.1.

Proof.

A Morse member. Write P0​(T)=T+∑j=2n−2λj​TjP_{0}(T)=T+\sum_{j=2}^{n-2}\lambda_{j}T^{j} for the fixed part of (1). Set r=0r=0, q=ε−(n−1)q=\varepsilon^{-(n-1)}, and T=ε​zT=\varepsilon z. Then

q​Tn+P0​(T)ε=zn+z+∑j=2n−2λj​εj−1​zj.\frac{qT^{n}+P_{0}(T)}{\varepsilon}=z^{n}+z+\sum_{j=2}^{n-2}\lambda_{j}\varepsilon^{j-1}z^{j}.

At ε=0\varepsilon=0 this is zn+zz^{n}+z. Its n−1n-1 critical points satisfy zn−1=−1/nz^{n-1}=-1/n; they are simple, and their critical values z⁡(zn−1+1)=(n−1)​z/nz(z^{n-1}+1)=(n-1)z/n are distinct. Both properties are open, so they persist for sufficiently small nonzero ε\varepsilon. Fix such a value of qq. Then g⁡(T)=q​Tn+P0​(T)g(T)=qT^{n}+P_{0}(T) is Morse.

The root group. Along the line {r=0,q​ fixed}\{r=0,\ q\text{ fixed}\} in the target, the roots of (1) are the points of g−1​(b)g^{-1}(b). The fundamental group of the bb-line minus the critical values is generated by loops around them, whose monodromy consists of transpositions. Since 𝔸T1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{T} is connected, the generated group is transitive. A transitive subgroup of SnS_{n} generated by transpositions is SnS_{n}. The monodromy along the line is a subgroup of the root monodromy over the whole target, which is therefore SnS_{n} as well.

The valuation. At a critical value b0b_{0}, the polynomial g⁡(T)−b0g(T)-b_{0} has exactly one double root and n−2n-2 simple roots. Along the bb-line the discriminant of g⁡(T)−bg(T)-b is a constant multiple of ∏(b−bj)\prod(b-b_{j}) over the critical values bjb_{j}, so it has a simple zero at b0b_{0}. Hence the discriminant hypersurface Δ\Delta is smooth at this point and transverse to the line, and its divisorial valuation vΔv_{\Delta} on kk satisfies vΔ​(disc⁡P)=1v_{\Delta}(\disc P)=1. Modulo vΔv_{\Delta}, PP has one double root t0t_{0} and n−2n-2 simple roots. Over the completion k^\hat{k} of kk at vΔv_{\Delta}, Hensel’s lemma therefore factors P=Q​R~P=Q\tilde{R}, with QQ quadratic reducing to a multiple of (T−t0)2(T-t_{0})^{2} and R~\tilde{R} separable modulo vΔv_{\Delta} and coprime to T−t0T-t_{0}. The roots of R~\tilde{R} generate an unramified extension, and their residues are distinct from each other and from t0t_{0}. Since the resultant of QQ and R~\tilde{R} and the discriminant of R~\tilde{R} are units, disc⁡Q\disc Q has value one. It is not a square in k^\hat{k}, so QQ is irreducible and generates a ramified quadratic extension. Hence any extension ww of vΔv_{\Delta} to k~\tilde{k}, normalized with value group ℤ\mathbb{Z}, has ramification index two, and w⁡((t1−t2)2)=2w\bigl((t_{1}-t_{2})^{2}\bigr)=2 for the two roots t1,t2t_{1},t_{2} of QQ. So t1−t2t_{1}-t_{2} is a uniformizer, while qq and all other root differences are units. This is the required valuation. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

For a completely fixed tuple, the target field is ℂ⁡(r,q,b)\mathbb{C}(r,q,b), and Lemmas 4.2 and 4.1 give the group GnG_{n}. For a partial descent or the original map, the target has additional free lower coefficients. Fix them arbitrarily to obtain the same Morse line. Its root monodromy still gives SnS_{n}, and its transverse simple branch point gives a pair valuation for the larger target field. The upper bound from (14) holds over every base field. Thus the group is GnG_{n} in every case. ∎

5 The finite normalization and its affine open

5.1 Overview

The source of a non-invertible Keller map is not finite over its target: sheets escape to infinity over the nonproperness locus. The finite normalization ZZ adds these escaped sheets back as divisors. Here ZZ has a transparent description: its points are all pairs consisting of a projective root of the target polynomial and a marking, with no simplicity condition. Two charts suffice, one for finite roots and one near the root at infinity, and the second is already an affine space. The source is the open set of pairs with a simple root, except that the root t=0t=0 keeps only the marking a=1a=1. So the missing divisors are the critical divisor, where the root is multiple, and the m−1m-1 divisors {t=0,a=ζ}\{t=0,\ a=\zeta\} with ζ≠1\zeta\neq 1.

Fix a successive coefficient slice Y≃𝔸dY\simeq\mathbb{A}^{d}. In (1) the symbols λj\lambda_{j} now denote either fixed complex numbers or the remaining independent coordinates. Let I⊂Y×ℙ1I\subset Y\times\mathbb{P}^{1} be the incidence variety of projective roots of the degree-nn homogenization of PP, with homogeneous coordinates [X1:X0][X_{1}:X_{0}] and t=X1/X0t=X_{1}/X_{0}. Since the coefficient of X1​X0n−1X_{1}X_{0}^{n-1} is one, that binary form never vanishes identically. Thus I→YI\to Y is finite flat of degree nn: it is a relative degree-nn effective divisor on ℙY1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{Y}.

5.2 Two charts and smoothness

On the finite-root chart define the cover by

P⁡(t)=0,am=P′​(t).P(t)=0,\qquad a^{m}=P^{\prime}(t).

On the infinity chart put Q⁡(u)=un​P​(1/u)Q(u)=u^{n}P(1/u) and define it by

Q⁡(u)=0,vm=−Q′​(u).Q(u)=0,\qquad v^{m}=-Q^{\prime}(u).

On the overlap u=1/tu=1/t, differentiating Q⁡(u)=un​P​(1/u)Q(u)=u^{n}P(1/u) and using P⁡(1/u)=0P(1/u)=0 gives

−Q′​(u)=un−2​P′​(1/u),so we glue byv=u​a.-Q^{\prime}(u)=u^{n-2}P^{\prime}(1/u),\qquad\text{so we glue by}\quad v=ua. (15)

These formulas define a finite flat degree-mm cover Z→IZ\to I. Consequently π:Z→Y\pi:Z\to Y is finite flat of degree n​mnm. The picture, with generic degrees indicated, is

𝔸d≃U⸦⟶Z→𝑚I→𝑛Y.\mathbb{A}^{d}\simeq U\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow Z\xrightarrow{\ m\ }I\xrightarrow{\ n\ }Y.

The open immersion on the left is identified below.

Write

Q0​(u)=∑j=2n−2λj​un−j+un−1−b​un,Q_{0}(u)=\sum_{j=2}^{n-2}\lambda_{j}u^{n-j}+u^{n-1}-bu^{n},

so that Q=q+r​u+Q0Q=q+ru+Q_{0}. The two equations of the infinity chart can be solved for rr and qq:

r=−vm−Q0′​(u),q=u​vm+u​Q0′​(u)−Q0​(u).r=-v^{m}-Q_{0}^{\prime}(u),\qquad q=uv^{m}+uQ_{0}^{\prime}(u)-Q_{0}(u). (16)

Hence the infinity chart is an affine space V≃𝔸dV\simeq\mathbb{A}^{d}, with coordinates u,v,bu,v,b and the free lower coefficients.

The complement of VV in ZZ lies over the root t=0t=0, where −b=P⁡(0)=0-b=P(0)=0 and am=P′​(0)=1a^{m}=P^{\prime}(0)=1. At these points the derivatives of the two equations P⁡(t)=0P(t)=0 and am−P′​(t)=0a^{m}-P^{\prime}(t)=0 with respect to (b,a)(b,a) form a triangular matrix with diagonal (−1,m​am−1)(-1,ma^{m-1}), which is invertible. So ZZ is smooth there, with local coordinates given by tt and the remaining target coordinates. In particular t=0t=0 is a divisor near every point of Z∖VZ\setminus V, so this complement contains no component of ZZ. Thus VV is dense. Since VV is integral and ZZ is smooth, ZZ is integral too.

By (7), the function field of ZZ is the source field of the polynomial map. A finite normal model with this field is the normalization of YY in that extension. This proves the first assertion of Theorem 1.3.

Holding bb and the free lower coefficients fixed, the chart determinant is especially simple:

det∂(r,q)∂(u,v)=m​v2​m−1.\det\frac{\partial(r,q)}{\partial(u,v)}=mv^{2m-1}. (17)

It follows by differentiating (16); the two terms involving u​Q0′′uQ_{0}^{\prime\prime} cancel.

5.3 The source open and every missing divisor

The source embeds in ZZ. The original source maps to II by [x:p][x:p], whose entries never vanish together. Its lifts to ZZ are a=1/pa=1/p where p≠0p\neq 0, and v=1/xv=1/x where x≠0x\neq 0; they agree by (15). The chart equations hold by (8) where x​p≠0xp\neq 0, and hence everywhere by continuity. This morphism is birational, and quasi-finite since its fibres are contained in fibres of the Keller map. Zariski’s Main Theorem, with the normal target ZZ, makes it an open immersion [12]. The same argument applies after the polynomial coordinate descents. Denote its image by UU.

The part inside VV. Put V∘=V∖{v=0}V^{\circ}=V\setminus\{v=0\}. We show U∩V=V∘U\cap V=V^{\circ}. The chart VV is the locus where the root is not [0:1][0:1], so a source point in VV has x≠0x\neq 0, hence v=1/x≠0v=1/x\neq 0. Conversely, let (u,v,b,…)∈V∘(u,v,b,\ldots)\in V^{\circ}. The reconstruction is

x=1/v,y=u−v,x=1/v,\qquad y=u-v, (18)

since u=p/x=1/x+yu=p/x=1/x+y. (For n=3n=3 the list is just A0A_{0}.) This includes the points u=0u=0, which are the simple roots at infinity.

The part outside VV. The remaining points have t=0t=0, a=ζ∈μma=\zeta\in\mu_{m} and b=0b=0. Source points with t=0t=0 have x=0x=0 and a=1/p=1a=1/p=1, so only the branch a=1a=1 can be retained. It is: near that branch,

(a−1)​(1+a+⋯+am−1)=P′​(t)−1,(a-1)(1+a+\cdots+a^{m-1})=P^{\prime}(t)-1,

and P′​(t)−1P^{\prime}(t)-1 is divisible by tt, while the factor in parentheses is a unit near a=1a=1. So y=(1−a)/ty=(1-a)/t is regular there, as are x=t/ax=t/a and, by the unit determinant p2​n−3p^{2n-3}, the zjz_{j}. On every branch a=ζ≠1a=\zeta\neq 1, the function y=(1−a)/ty=(1-a)/t has a simple pole, so these branches are omitted.

It follows that the whole omitted boundary is

Z∖U=Ecrit⊔⨆ζ∈μm∖{1}Eζ,Ecrit={v=0}⊂V,Eζ={t=0,a=ζ}.Z\setminus U=E_{\mathrm{crit}}\ \sqcup\!\bigsqcup_{\zeta\in\mu_{m}\setminus\{1\}}E_{\zeta},\qquad E_{\mathrm{crit}}=\{v=0\}\subset V,\quad E_{\zeta}=\{t=0,a=\zeta\}. (19)

On VV, the equations Q⁡(u)=0=Q′​(u)Q(u)=0=Q^{\prime}(u) show that EcritE_{\mathrm{crit}} is the locus of multiple projective roots. Each component is 𝔸d−1\mathbb{A}^{d-1}: EcritE_{\mathrm{crit}} is a coordinate hyperplane of VV, and EζE_{\zeta} maps isomorphically onto the hyperplane {b=0}\{b=0\} of YY. The components are pairwise disjoint, because P′​(0)=1P^{\prime}(0)=1 and so the zero root is never multiple. The retained zero branch a=1a=1 is another copy of {b=0}\{b=0\} inside UU.

5.4 Ramification and fibre defects

Let Δ⊂Y\Delta\subset Y be the reduced binary discriminant. The image of EcritE_{\mathrm{crit}} consists of precisely the polynomials with a multiple projective root. Thus Δ\Delta is irreducible, as the finite image of the irreducible EcritE_{\mathrm{crit}}. The Morse line in Lemma 4.2 shows that its generic member has just one double root. Hence Ecrit→ΔE_{\mathrm{crit}}\to\Delta is finite and birational, and, since EcritE_{\mathrm{crit}} is smooth, it is the normalization of Δ\Delta.

At a generic double root the incidence map I→YI\to Y has ramification index two. The cyclic cover has index mm there, because its defining derivative has a simple zero on II. Therefore EcritE_{\mathrm{crit}} has ramification index 2​m2m and residue degree one over Δ\Delta, consistent with (17), whose zero of order 2​m−12m-1 along v=0v=0 is the ramification divisor. At each EζE_{\zeta}, the derivatives with respect to (t,a)(t,a) in the finite chart form the invertible matrix (10−P′′​(0)m​ζm−1)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ -P^{\prime\prime}(0)&m\zeta^{m-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr), so the map is unramified there and has residue degree one.

Over a general point of Δ\Delta, 2​m2m sheets are missing from UU, counted with multiplicity. Over a general point of b=0b=0, m−1m-1 sheets are missing, although those omitted branches are unramified. Thus ramification alone cannot detect the affine-source defect. A simple root at infinity is retained, so q=0q=0 is not an additional boundary image. For m=1m=1 there are no omitted zero-root branches.

5.5 Picard group and homotopy type

Since U≃𝔸dU\simeq\mathbb{A}^{d} is factorial, any divisor on ZZ becomes principal on UU. Subtracting that principal divisor leaves a divisor supported on (19). If a linear combination of these boundary divisors were principal, its rational function would restrict to a unit on UU, hence a constant, and the combination would be zero. Smoothness identifies Weil and Cartier class groups, proving

Pic⁡(Z)=⨁E⊂Z∖Uℤ⁡[E]≃ℤm.\Pic(Z)=\bigoplus_{E\subset Z\setminus U}\mathbb{Z}[E]\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{m}. (20)

5.6 Rational and polynomial deck groups

For a transitive monodromy action on a generic fibre Ω\Omega, the automorphism group of the source field over the target field is the centralizer of the monodromy group in Sym⁡(Ω)\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega). A permutation commuting with the monodromy is determined by the image of one point, and that image must be fixed by the stabilizer of the point. In GnG_{n}, the stabilizer of a pair (t1,a1)(t_{1},a_{1}) consists of the elements with σ⁡(1)=1\sigma(1)=1 and ζ1=1\zeta_{1}=1. It fixes the mm points (t1,ζ​a1)(t_{1},\zeta a_{1}) of the same root block, and no other point, since it contains elements moving tjt_{j} to tkt_{k} for any j,k≠1j,k\neq 1 (for even nn, adjust some ζk\zeta_{k} with k≠1k\neq 1 to satisfy the sign condition). Thus the centralizer has at most mm elements. The global cyclic action already gives mm, so the rational deck group is exactly μm\mu_{m}.

Every nonidentity element moves the retained zero-root branch a=1a=1 to an omitted branch a=ζa=\zeta, so none preserves UU. A polynomial deck automorphism of the source would induce one of these field automorphisms, extend to ZZ by normality, and preserve UU. So only the identity is possible. This finishes the proof of Theorem 1.3.

Remark 5.1.

For n=4n=4 we have m=2m=2, and the picture is as small as possible: Z∖U=Ecrit⊔E−1Z\setminus U=E_{\mathrm{crit}}\sqcup E_{-1}, where E−1E_{-1} is the branch of the root t=0t=0 with marking a=−1a=-1. Thus Pic⁡(Z)≃ℤ2\Pic(Z)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{2} and Z⁡(ℂ)≃S2∨S2Z(\mathbb{C})\simeq S^{2}\vee S^{2}, and the rational deck transformation a↦−aa\mapsto-a exchanges the retained zero branch with E−1E_{-1}.

Remark 5.2.

Triviality of the polynomial deck group holds for every complex affine-space Keller map. That group embeds in the automorphism group of a finite field extension, so is finite. A deck automorphism fixing a point is the identity near it by local analytic invertibility, hence everywhere, so the group acts freely. For the quotient, multiplicativity of the compactly supported Euler characteristic gives 1=χc​(𝔸d)=|G|​χc​(𝔸d/G)1=\chi_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{d})=|G|\chi_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{d}/G), forcing |G|=1|G|=1. Our boundary calculation describes explicitly why the nontrivial rational deck transformations fail to preserve the source.

6 Sections by subvarieties and factorized sectors

Restricting a Keller map to the preimage of a subvariety of its target is the natural way to look for lower-dimensional examples. If Γ⊂Y\Gamma\subset Y is a smooth subvariety, the preimage F−1​(Γ)F^{-1}(\Gamma) is smooth and étale over Γ\Gamma, but it can have several components, none of which need be an affine space. This section describes these components, which we call sectors, exactly. Everything follows from Theorem 1.3 by base change.

Throughout, FF, YY and U⊂ZU\subset Z are as in Theorem 1.3, with F=KnF=K_{n} and Y=𝔸nY=\mathbb{A}^{n} the full target, and m=n−2m=n-2. For a point η∈Y\eta\in Y write PηP_{\eta} for its target polynomial and Pη,h​(X1,X0)=X0n​Pη​(X1/X0)P_{\eta,h}(X_{1},X_{0})=X_{0}^{n}P_{\eta}(X_{1}/X_{0}) for its degree-nn homogenization, so that t=X1/X0t=X_{1}/X_{0} and a source point has root [X1:X0]=[x:p][X_{1}:X_{0}]=[x:p]. We write ∂1,∂0\partial_{1},\partial_{0} for the partial derivatives in X1,X0X_{1},X_{0}. The idea of the section is simple. A sector over Γ\Gamma selects, over each point of Γ\Gamma, one simple root of the target polynomial together with a marking. If the target polynomial factors over Γ\Gamma, the selected root belongs to one factor GG, and the marking is then controlled by GG alone.

7 Stable comparison and specialization

Two polynomial maps are stably left–right equivalent if, after adjoining enough identity coordinates to each, polynomial automorphisms of source and target identify them. Their generic field extensions are then isomorphic after adjoining independent transcendental variables. The normal closure and its permutation action on the source embeddings are unchanged by such an extension. Generic permutation monodromy is therefore a stable invariant.

The finite normalization together with its distinguished affine source open is also intrinsic. Indeed, if ℬ\mathcal{B} is the integral closure of a target coordinate ring 𝒜\mathcal{A} in the source function field ℒ\mathcal{L}, then ℬ⁡[s]\mathcal{B}[s] is the integral closure of 𝒜⁡[s]\mathcal{A}[s] in ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s). It is normal and integral over 𝒜⁡[s]\mathcal{A}[s]; conversely, an element integral over 𝒜⁡[s]\mathcal{A}[s] is integral over ℬ⁡[s]\mathcal{B}[s] and hence belongs to it. This observation, also used in the normalization framework of [16], transports the boundary and its ramification and residue degrees under stable equivalence.

Proposition 7.1.

Let a degree-NN map to 𝔸A,B,C3\mathbb{A}^{3}_{A,B,C} have source function field generated over ℂ⁡(A,B,C)\mathbb{C}(A,B,C) by an element ww with minimal polynomial

ℋ⁡(w)−B​C​w+c​A​C2,ℋ∈ℂ⁡[w],deg⁡ℋ=N≥2,c∈ℂ∗.\mathcal{H}(w)-BCw+cAC^{2},\qquad\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{C}[w],\quad\deg\mathcal{H}=N\geq 2,\quad c\in\mathbb{C}^{*}.

Its generic monodromy over ℂ⁡(A,B,C)\mathbb{C}(A,B,C) is SNS_{N}.

Proof.

On C≠0C\neq 0, put B′=B​CB^{\prime}=BC and A′=−c​A​C2A^{\prime}=-cAC^{2}. Together with CC these are independent coordinates, so the polynomial becomes ℋ⁡(w)−B′​w−A′\mathcal{H}(w)-B^{\prime}w-A^{\prime}, with the extra independent variable CC. If hNh_{N} is the leading coefficient of ℋ\mathcal{H}, set B′=−hN​ρN−1B^{\prime}=-h_{N}\rho^{N-1} and w=ρ​zw=\rho z, and divide by hN​ρNh_{N}\rho^{N}. As ρ\rho tends to infinity, ℋ⁡(w)−B′​w\mathcal{H}(w)-B^{\prime}w tends in these coordinates to zN+zz^{N}+z, which is Morse. So for some value of B′B^{\prime} the polynomial ℋ⁡(w)−B′​w\mathcal{H}(w)-B^{\prime}w is Morse, and, as in Lemma 4.2, the connected cover of the A′A^{\prime}-line has monodromy generated by transpositions, giving SNS_{N}. The extra transcendental variable does not change that group. ∎

The antiderivative presentation and its full symmetric monodromy are Theorems A–B of [9]; see also [15]. The proof is included to make the comparison independent of a classification of other constructions. For n≥4n\geq 4, GnG_{n} is imprimitive on N=n​mN=nm letters, whereas SNS_{N} is primitive. Proposition 7.1 and stable invariance prove Corollary 1.4. The argument distinguishes single weighted lifts. It makes no assertion about their compositions, or about all cancellation or quadratic-gauge maps. The use of this stable invariant, including an explicit imprimitive composition example, precedes this paper [17].

7.1 An exact overlap with power-weighted lifts

The power-weighted lifts of [1] generalize the ordinary weighted lifts of Proposition 7.1; when the weight parameter is greater than one, their source field has an additional cyclic stage, so Proposition 7.1 does not apply to them. The degree-eight map F2,3=(F1,F2,F3)F_{2,3}=(F_{1},F_{2},F_{3}) of [1] can be written, with α=x2​y\alpha=x^{2}y, as

F1\displaystyle F_{1} =z​(1+α)4+x​y23​(5​α3+17​α2+20​α+8),\displaystyle=z(1+\alpha)^{4}+\frac{xy^{2}}{3}(5\alpha^{3}+17\alpha^{2}+20\alpha+8),
F2\displaystyle F_{2} =4​x​z​(1+α)3+y3​(20​α3+48​α2+33​α+2),\displaystyle=4xz(1+\alpha)^{3}+\frac{y}{3}(20\alpha^{3}+48\alpha^{2}+33\alpha+2),
F3\displaystyle F_{3} =−x4​z+x3​(3−5​α).\displaystyle=-x^{4}z+\frac{x}{3}(3-5\alpha).

Use the source coordinates (x,u,w)=(x,s3,s4)(x,u,w)=(x,s_{3},s_{4}) of E4,0E_{4,0} from Section 3, with outputs (r,q,b)(r,q,b). Direct substitution gives

E4,0∘Ψ=Λ∘F2,3,Ψ(x,y,z)=(x,y,−2z−4x3y3−203xy2),Λ(A,B,C)=(−B,3A,C).\begin{gathered}E_{4,0}\circ\Psi=\Lambda\circ F_{2,3},\\ \Psi(x,y,z)=\left(x,y,-2z-4x^{3}y^{3}-\frac{20}{3}xy^{2}\right),\qquad\Lambda(A,B,C)=(-B,3A,C).\end{gathered} (24)

Both are polynomial automorphisms: the third coordinate of Ψ−1\Psi^{-1} is −w/2−2x3u3−(10/3)xu2-w/2-2x^{3}u^{3}-(10/3)xu^{2}, and Λ−1​(r,q,b)=(q/3,−r,b)\Lambda^{-1}(r,q,b)=(q/3,-r,b). Thus the equivalence requires no stabilization. The determinants detJ​Ψ=−2\det J\Psi=-2 and detΛ=3\det\Lambda=3 are consistent with detJ​E4,0=1\det JE_{4,0}=1 and detJF2,3=−2/3\det JF_{2,3}=-2/3, since 1⋅(−2)=3⋅(−2/3)1\cdot(-2)=3\cdot(-2/3). The exact verification supplement checks every component of (24) against the recursive descent construction.

Consequently the degree-eight map E4,0E_{4,0} is already present in the literature, and the order-192192 group computed here also describes that map. No equivalence with higher power-weighted members or with the nonzero parameter descents is asserted. In particular the ordinary-weighted distinction cannot be strengthened to exclude all power-weighted lifts.

7.2 Nonlinear sections

The results above hold for every fixed coordinate parameter because the polynomial charts and the Morse line were proved uniformly. For a general nonlinear target subvariety Γ→Y\Gamma\to Y, Proposition 6.1 still describes the preimage UΓU_{\Gamma} exactly, as an open subset of Z×YΓZ\times_{Y}\Gamma. But this base change can be reducible or singular, normalization need not commute with it, and a component of UΓU_{\Gamma} need not be an affine space. Proposition 6.4 identifies such a component with an open subset of a Kummer cover of the simple-root locus of one factor; deciding whether it is an affine space requires further geometric input.

The standard local cyclic model illustrates how degrees can drop. A cover am=sa^{m}=s pulled back by s=zℓs=z^{\ell} becomes am=zℓa^{m}=z^{\ell}. If g=gcd⁡(m,ℓ)g=\gcd(m,\ell), there are gg branches over ℂ\mathbb{C}, and the normalization of each branch has degree m/gm/g over the zz-line. For ℓ=m\ell=m this cyclic stage splits into degree-one branches. This explains a possible drop in component degree, but does not make the entire marked-root map injective or give a polynomial affine-space chart for the new source.

7.3 Further questions

The generic group, boundary count, Picard rank and homotopy type are constant across the fixed-coordinate parameters, so they cannot distinguish the maps En,λE_{n,\lambda} from one another up to stable equivalence. The actual maps of the boundary divisors and the intersections of their images provide finer candidate invariants. Other questions include monodromy on nonlinear target graphs and the behaviour of their normalized boundary under tangential specialization. These require arguments beyond the coordinate-descent theorem.

8 Exact verification and scope

The proofs establish the uniform statements. Symbolic computations provide independent checks of formulas, finite examples and their implementation; they are not substitutes for proofs in unbounded dimension or for the topological gluing argument.

The accompanying scripts perform the following focused checks:

  1. 1.

    reconstruction on the finite, zero and infinity charts, together with all multiplicity partitions in a finite range;

  2. 2.

    the first polynomial coordinate chart and its inverse, the completion lemma, iterated descents through n=8n=8, an all-parameter n=5n=5 calculation, and a transported collision;

  3. 3.

    the derivative-product identity, the integer Smith form of the pair-valuation matrix, exact abstract permutation-group orders, and Morse critical-value checks;

  4. 4.

    the two normalization charts, their overlap, the ramification determinant, substitution of original source maps, and cyclic specialization controls;

  5. 5.

    the polynomial identity with the published power-weighted degree-eight map, its inverse source chart, determinant and collision;

  6. 6.

    the homogeneous derivative identity (∂1Ph)​(x,p)=p(\partial_{1}P_{h})(x,p)=p for n≤8n\leq 8, the balanced-factor resultant identity, and numerical reconstruction of every source point over random factorized targets, together with p=Hh​(x,p)​∂1Gh​(x,p)p=H_{h}(x,p)\,\partial_{1}G_{h}(x,p) at each of them (Section 6);

  7. 7.

    the identities derived in the text of Sections 2 and 3: Lemma 2.1 for n≤9n\leq 9, the two determinant factors in Proposition 2.2, the n=3n=3 example, the first chart and its boundary offsets for n≤8n\leq 8, the explicit map E4,0E_{4,0}, the model case of Lemma 3.1, and, for Proposition 3.2, the dependence of the offsets and the inverse-boundary formula (13) for n=5,6n=5,6, and the slopes −23,−32,23,32-\frac{2}{3},-\frac{3}{2},\frac{2}{3},\frac{3}{2} for n=8n=8.

The scripts use only SymPy. The runner run_all.py executes all of them and writes a manifest with their hashes, exit statuses and run times; a complete run takes about thirteen minutes.

Data availability.

The scripts, the runner and a reference run form a self-contained supplement under the Apache License 2.0. Its README maps each script to the statements it checks. The supplement is distributed as the ancillary files of this paper on arXiv.
